concepts.name: Drain of Wealth Theory: Origins and Evolution
key_dimensions: Dadabhai Naoroji's 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901) — core arguments and quantification methodology
Distinction between 'home charges' and productive investment — what counted as 'drain' vs. legitimate trade
R.C. Dutt and M.G. Ranade's refinements vs. Naoroji's original formulation — where they agreed and diverged
UPSC trap: British counter-argument (trade surplus as evidence of prosperity) and nationalist rebuttal

concepts.name: Swadeshi Movement (1905–1908): Economic vs. Political Dimensions
key_dimensions: Immediate trigger (Partition of Bengal) vs. deeper economic grievances — how economics and politics intertwined
Boycott of British goods as an economic weapon — distinction from later Non-Cooperation's boycott strategy
Constructive Swadeshi: promotion of indigenous mills, banks (like Bank of Bengal controversies), and national education
UPSC trap: Moderate vs. Extremist approaches within Swadeshi — Gokhale's reservations vs. Tilak/Lajpat Rai's maximalism

concepts.name: Early Indian Nationalist Critique of Colonial Economic Policy: The 'Three Schools'
key_dimensions: Dadabhai Naoroji (drain theory), R.C. Dutt (deindustrialisation + agrarian critique), M.G. Ranade (state-led industrialisation) — distinguishing their core theses
Ranade's departure from laissez-faire: argument for protective tariffs and state intervention — contrast with British free trade ideology
G.V. Joshi and Gopal Krishna Gokhale's contributions to economic nationalist discourse — often overlooked names
UPSC trap: Conflating all three as identical — each had a distinct policy prescription beyond just criticising the British

concepts.name: Deindustrialisation Thesis: Debate and Evidence
key_dimensions: R.C. Dutt's argument in 'Economic History of India' — specific industries cited (textiles, iron, shipbuilding)
Mechanism: one-way free trade, machine competition, and destruction of artisan guilds vs. British claim of 'natural obsolescence'
Revisionist challenge: Morris D. Morris's counter-data on urban wage labour growth — why UPSC may test this nuance
UPSC trap: Deindustrialisation ≠ complete destruction — regional variations (Bengal handloom vs. Bombay mill growth) and the partial nature of the process

concepts.name: Indian National Congress's Early Economic Agenda (1885–1905)
key_dimensions: Economic resolutions at early INC sessions — specific demands (reduction of home charges, tariff protection, Indianisation of services)
The 'Mendicancy' critique by later nationalists — why Extremists called early Congress economically timid
Gokhale's role in economic debates in the Imperial Legislative Council — bridge between petition politics and data-driven advocacy
UPSC trap: Early Congress was NOT purely political — its economic agenda is frequently tested as a lesser-known dimension

concepts.name: Protective Tariff Controversy: Cotton Excise Duty
key_dimensions: British imposition of cotton excise duty (1894) to 'equalise' competition between Lancashire mills and Indian mills — the asymmetry of 'free trade'
Indian nationalist response: this as proof of colonial economic subjugation and conflict of interest in policy-making
Bombay Mill owners' agitation — confluence of Indian capitalist interests and nationalist politics
UPSC trap: The excise duty was presented as 'neutral' by Britain but effectively subsidised British exports — the ideological sleight of hand in free trade arguments

concepts.name: Rise of Indian Industrial Capitalism and its Nationalist Alignment
key_dimensions: Tata Iron and Steel Company (1907) as a symbol of economic nationalism — Swadeshi capital mobilisation and public subscription campaign
Relationship between Indian business houses (Tata, Birla) and the Congress — symbiotic but tension-ridden
FICCI (1927) founding — institutionalisation of Indian capitalist interest in nationalist politics
UPSC trap: Indian capitalists supported nationalism but NOT always Congress's socialist/land reform agenda — the internal contradiction within the nationalist coalition

concepts.name: Boycott as an Economic Strategy: Typology and Effectiveness
key_dimensions: Three distinct boycott movements: 1905 Swadeshi, 1920–22 Non-Cooperation, 1930–34 Civil Disobedience — different targets, scope, and outcomes
Economic impact measured: fall in British textile imports during each phase — where it worked and where it failed
Social limits of boycott: urban middle class vs. rural poor who could not afford Swadeshi goods
UPSC trap: 1905 boycott was primarily Bengal-centric; 1920 boycott added foreign cloth + liquor; 1930 added salt — the escalating and widening scope is a key distinction

concepts.name: National Planning Idea: Pre-Independence Intellectual Roots
key_dimensions: M. Visvesvaraya's 'Planned Economy for India' (1934) — first systematic planning blueprint by an Indian
Congress's National Planning Committee (1938) under Nehru — its composition, mandate, and sub-committees
Bombay Plan (1944) — Indian industrialists' plan: who authored it, what it proposed, and why it is significant as a capitalist document endorsing state intervention
UPSC trap: Bombay Plan is often mistaken as a Congress/government document — it was authored by private industrialists (Tata, Birla, Thakurdas) yet endorsed planning

concepts.name: Gandhi's Economic Philosophy as Nationalist Response
key_dimensions: Charkha and Khadi as economic tools — logic of village self-sufficiency vs. industrial capitalism, and the employment argument
Gandhi's critique of modern industrial civilisation ('Hind Swaraj', 1909) — not merely anti-British but anti-industrial
Trusteeship theory — Gandhi's alternative to both capitalism and socialism as a nationalist economic framework
UPSC trap: Gandhi was NOT anti-technology in all forms — he opposed large-scale factory production displacing labour, not technology per se; he supported some machinery

concepts.name: Land Revenue Systems and Agrarian Economic Nationalism
key_dimensions: Permanent Settlement (Zamindari), Ryotwari, and Mahalwari — nationalist critique of each as instruments of surplus extraction
R.C. Dutt's specific critique of the revenue demand as the primary cause of Indian poverty and famines
Peasant movements with economic nationalist overtones: Deccan Riots (1875), Champaran (1917), Bardoli (1928) — each with distinct economic grievances
UPSC trap: Permanent Settlement is often seen as 'Bengal-only' — but its logic of property rights and rent extraction influenced nationalist thinking about land reform nationwide

concepts.name: Famine Policy Critique and Economic Nationalist Discourse
key_dimensions: Dadabhai Naoroji and Digby's use of famine data to quantify drain — famine as proof of impoverishment, not natural disaster
Famine Commission Reports (1880, 1901) vs. nationalist critique — where official and nationalist interpretations diverged
Mike Davis's 'Late Victorian Holocausts' thesis (modern echo of nationalist argument) — UPSC may test awareness of historiographical continuity
UPSC trap: Nationalists argued famines were policy-made (export of food during famine, high revenue demand); British argued they were weather-driven — the political economy of famine interpretation

concepts.name: Indian Currency and Exchange Rate Policy as a Nationalist Issue
key_dimensions: The rupee-sterling exchange rate controversy — fixing the rate at 1s 4d (1898) and its impact on Indian exports and debt burden
Nationalist argument: exchange rate policy served British creditor interests over Indian producer interests
Gokhale and later nationalists in the Legislative Council demanding Indian control over monetary policy
UPSC trap: Currency policy is a less-tested but high-yield area — the link between gold standard, home charges, and economic drain is a sophisticated analytical question

concepts.name: Railways: Nationalist Ambivalence and Economic Critique
key_dimensions: British argument (railways as 'gift of civilisation') vs. nationalist counter (railways built at guaranteed profit to British investors, served extraction not integration)
Dadabhai Naoroji's specific critique: railway finance added to home charges; Indian investors excluded from guaranteed returns
Gandhi's critique in 'Hind Swaraj' — railways spread plague and enabled military control, not development

UPSC trap: Nationalists were NOT uniformly anti-railway — Ranade and later Congress saw railways as necessary for industrialisation but demanded Indianisation of management and end of profit guarantees

concepts.name: The 'Imperial Preference' System and Indian Economic Nationalism in the Interwar Period
key_dimensions: Ottawa Agreement (1932) — how imperial preference forced India to give tariff concessions to British goods, limiting protectionist policy
Indian industrialists' and nationalists' opposition to Ottawa — conflict between London's imperial economic interests and Indian developmental needs
Simon Commission and Round Table Conferences — economic demands (fiscal autonomy, tariff autonomy) as core nationalist positions
UPSC trap: Fiscal autonomy demand preceded political autonomy demand in some nationalist formulations — the sequencing of economic vs. political independence claims

concepts.name: Nehru's Socialist Economic Nationalism: 'Discovery of India' to NPC
key_dimensions: Nehru's synthesis of nationalism and socialism — critique of both colonial capitalism AND Gandhi's village-economy model
National Planning Committee (1938): Nehru's vision of heavy industry, electrification, and scientific planning as the nationalist economic alternative
Contradiction between Nehru's socialism and Congress's dependence on big business funding — the internal tension
UPSC trap: NPC was dissolved by WWII but its reports influenced post-independence planning — the intellectual continuity between 1938 NPC and 1950 Planning Commission is a key linkage

concepts.name: Economic Nationalism in Regional Contexts: Bengal, Maharashtra, and Punjab
key_dimensions: Bengal: Swadeshi industrial enterprises (Bengal Chemical, National Soap) — successes and failures, capital limitations
Maharashtra: Ranade's Poona Sarvajanik Sabha and economic reform agenda — decentralised industrialisation model
Punjab: Lala Lajpat Rai's economic writings and the Punjab National Bank as an instrument of economic nationalism
UPSC trap: Economic nationalism was NOT uniform — regional economic structures (jute in Bengal, cotton in Bombay, wheat in Punjab) shaped different nationalist economic priorities

concepts.name: The 'Poverty of India' Discourse: Data, Methodology, and Political Use
key_dimensions: Naoroji's per capita income calculation methodology — how he arrived at figures and why the methodology itself was politically significant
William Digby's 'Prosperous' British India (1901) — satirical use of data to rebut British claims, complementing Naoroji
Evolution from moral indictment to statistical economics — how Indian nationalists 'scientised' their economic critique
UPSC trap: The poverty discourse was a strategic choice — by using British government's own data, nationalists denied Britain the ability to dismiss the argument as emotional or unpatriotic

concepts.name: Economic Demands in the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34)
key_dimensions: The Eleven Demands (1930) — specifically economic ones: salt tax abolition, 50% reduction in military expenditure, protective tariff on foreign cloth, postal reservation bill
Salt as an economic symbol — why Gandhi chose salt (universal commodity, regressive tax, state monopoly) over other economic grievances
Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) — which economic demands were conceded, which were dropped, and nationalist criticism of the compromise
UPSC trap: The Eleven Demands contained BOTH economic and political elements — UPSC often tests whether candidates can identify the specifically economic demands and their logic

concepts.name: Post-War Economic Nationalism and the Transfer of Power Negotiations
key_dimensions: Sterling balances controversy (WWII) — India accumulated £1.3 billion in British debt; nationalist demand for conversion as settlement of the drain
Indian industrialists' shift: from seeking British market access to demanding protection from British competition in an independent India
Economic clauses in Cabinet Mission Plan and independence negotiations — continuity of economic dependency as a concern

UPSC trap: The sterling balances issue shows economic nationalism persisting into independence negotiations — it is often overlooked as a purely financial matter but was a direct descendant of the drain theory debate
